bases.routine: Period routine of a frontier post: reveille about 5:30, tattoo 21:00 (as T-3462 place.py); breakfast, a noon dinner and supper; children kept close by their mothers.
bases.close: After April no one left the garrison's vicinity without a guard (Wau-Bun) and the whites kept close to the fort (Quaife); so play is kept beside the quarters.
bases.indoors_14: On the 14th Potawatomi men were entering the fort and a council sat in the afternoon (Wau-Bun); mothers would keep small children in.
bases.winter: Winter and early spring 1812 at the family's own house: short days, most of the day indoors by the fire (period routine).

meta.coordinates: Local metres, as place.py. Footprints read with rotation_deg clockwise about the placement corner. Inside the stockade: the parade is E 1144.1-1159.6, N 213.0-229.5; the officers' barracks E 1138.5-1142.3, N 213.7-227.0; the commanding officer's E 1161.8-1165.8, N 218.2-227.3; the small house NE E 1162.1-1165.8, N 231.7-234.8. The Agency House is E 1060.9-1071.1, N 162.1-175.7. The children's play point on the parade (1151.2, 216.4) sits between the fatigue rank (E 1146.3) and the SE knot (1154.8, 215.1); the implementer should spread the children round it (radius about 1.2 m) as place.py spreads a knot.
meta.day_shape: Each child has "days": one entry per date range in which its home differs, with a plain day for the range and the 14 August specifics as their own entry. Infants carry infant_in_arms true and their outdoor spans carry figure "in_arms" and carried_by: they are drawn only in the carrier's arms, never standing.
meta.seasons: Winter (15 Feb) and early spring (to 7 April): the Kinzie, Burns and Lee children at their own houses. Spring (15 Apr) and summer (14 Aug): the Kinzie children in the fort, the Burns and Lee children at the Agency House. Fall (15 Oct): only the Ouilmette children (the garrison gone, the Kinzies at St Joseph).
meta.activity_vocabulary: activity uses the brief's list; children at play are "knot" (a group facing in, as place.py knots) or "sit"; "doing" says it is play.

people.name: John Harris Kinzie

present.basis: With the family in the fort from 7 April (Andreas p. 74) and in the boat on 15 August (Wau-Bun); no roll is taken on the 14th.

presence.basis: Born at Sandwich 7 July 1803; the family settled at Chicago in 1804 (year only; the household card's arrival). Left on the third day after the battle (Wau-Bun), 18 August.

age_1812.basis: Born 7 July 1803 (Kirkland), so 9 years 1 month on 14 August; Currey and Andreas both say nine.

looks.basis: Heritage: father of Scottish descent, born at Quebec; mother Eleanor (Lytle) of a Pennsylvania family. Fair skin, brown hair, light eyes. Colouring read off his own 1827 miniature (at 24). Height for age: the CDC 2000 stature-for-age table at the 10th centile for the age on 14 Aug 1812. Not a measurement. Why that centile: Steckel 1985 finds slave children below the first centile of modern standards and Komlos 2003 puts American apprentices of 14 at the 0.8th, while American adults reached about the 20th-30th; free children of a fed frontier household are set at the 10th, a prosperous trader's family.

infant_in_arms_1812.pieces: a long white cotton or linen gown (frock) reaching past the feet, a small cap, a shawl or blanket round it when carried; never drawn standing, only in an adult's arms or in a cradle indoors
infant_in_arms_1812.colours: white; the shawl or blanket brown, red or blue wool
infant_in_arms_1812.note: The Beecher frock (about 1813) was worn by an infant boy, so boys and girls are dressed alike. The cut is eastern; that a frontier baby wore the same in coarser cloth is inference (dress.json "Children 2-12 and infants").

child_frock_toddler_1812.pieces: unbreeched child of either sex, about 1 to 4: high-waisted frock to the ankle, short puffed or long sleeves, a cap or bare head, barefoot in summer or soft shoes; a pinafore over it for play
child_frock_toddler_1812.colours: white, or a small-figured printed cotton (pink, blue); garrison and militia children in coarser coloured cloth
child_frock_toddler_1812.note: Boys under about four are drawn in frocks: the Beecher frock was a boy's, and the Rutter boy of about six is already in a suit. The age at breeching is not recorded for anyone at Chicago; between three and six is our reading of those two pictures. Bare feet in summer rest on Krimmel's working boys (Philadelphia).

boy_skeleton_suit_1812.pieces: boy about 4 to 8: short jacket buttoned onto long high-waisted trousers (skeleton suit), white shirt with a wide frilled or plain collar; at work or play in summer, shirt and trousers with the jacket off, barefoot
boy_skeleton_suit_1812.colours: dark blue, tan-brown or green jacket and trousers; white shirt; garrison boys in drab or homespun
boy_skeleton_suit_1812.note: The Rutter boy (about 1805) is the skeleton suit; the Pixler boys (about 1815) show rural boys' short jackets and checked or spotted trousers.

boy_jacket_trousers_1812.pieces: boy about 8 to 13: short or cutaway jacket, waistcoat, long trousers, white shirt with collar open or a small frill, round hat out of doors; at chores in shirtsleeves and trousers, barefoot in summer
boy_jacket_trousers_1812.colours: jacket dark blue, brown or green; trousers plain, checked or spotted; hat black or straw
boy_jacket_trousers_1812.note: John H. Kinzie, a prosperous trader's son, in the better cloth; a soldier's or settler's boy in the same shapes, coarser.

girl_frock_pinafore_1812.pieces: girl about 4 to 13: high-waisted frock to the ankle (the older girl's a little longer), short sleeves in summer, a pinafore or apron over it for work, a sunbonnet or cap out of doors; shoes, or barefoot in summer for a working family
girl_frock_pinafore_1812.colours: frock white, or printed cotton (pink, blue, brown sprig); pinafore white or checked linen; bonnet white or straw
girl_frock_pinafore_1812.note: The frock is seen on the Rutter girl; the pinafore is our reconstruction, as dress.json already says. The Kinzie girls in the finer cloth; Isabella Cooper and the Lee girl in coarser.

girl_of_the_country_1812.pieces: a French or Metis girl of a trader's or carrier's household: short gown and petticoat cut small, a printed cotton handkerchief at the neck or round the head, moccasins
girl_of_the_country_1812.colours: short gown printed cotton (blue, red, brown); petticoat dark homespun or blue stroud; head handkerchief blue cotton; moccasins smoked tan leather
girl_of_the_country_1812.note: Wau-Bun's "ordinary dress of a French woman of the country" at Chicago in 1812 (PG 51737 lines 6474-6476: a short gown and petticoat, a blue cotton handkerchief round the head) cut down for a girl; Lambert for moccasins among the country people. No child of the Ouilmette or Mirandeau household is described. Anything of Potawatomi or Ottawa dress belongs to the Native-dress researcher and is not invented here.

boy_of_the_country_1812.pieces: a French or Metis boy of a trader's or carrier's household: calico shirt, loose trousers, moccasins, a red knitted cap or bare head, a sash in the cool of the year
boy_of_the_country_1812.colours: shirt printed or blue calico; trousers blue or natural linen; moccasins smoked tan; cap red
boy_of_the_country_1812.note: The engage's summer dress of dress.json cut down for a boy. Not evidenced for any boy at Chicago.

not_placed.why: Wau-Bun calls him "the boy" who ran down from Lee's Place on 7 April, but Quaife makes him one of the twelve militiamen, so on 14 August he is with the men. Handed to the researcher placing the militia and civilian men; if nobody places him, he is a youth (age not recorded) at the Agency House drawing arms with his father.

not_placed.name: Peter Bell
not_placed.why: Simmons 1896 has "Peter Bell, six years old" walking beside the wagon; T-3461 excluded him as disputed (garrison.json). Not placed until a second source puts him at Fort Dearborn.

not_placed.name: The Healds' son
not_placed.why: Born dead on 4 May 1812 (garrison.json); never a figure. On the spring Season date (15 April) Rebekah Heald is near her time.

not_placed.name: Mrs. Corbin's unborn child
not_placed.why: Not born; Quaife allows that Mrs. Corbin may have had no child at the post.

not_placed.name: Elizabeth, Josette and Sophie Ouilmette
not_placed.why: Elizabeth was born about 1813 (CPN Heritage Center page) and Josette was a child in 1831 (T-3461), so they are not in 1812; Sophie's birth is not known.

not_placed.name: The other Mirandeau children (Genevieve, Jean Baptiste Jr., Thomas)
not_placed.why: Andreas names them as Victoire's siblings with no ages or 1811-12 whereabouts; "some of us" lived in the Ouilmette house. Not placed.

not_placed.name: John B. Lalime (son of Noke-no-qua)
not_placed.why: Known only from the 1821 treaty grant (Quaife); neither his age nor his presence in 1812 is recorded (civilians.json). Jean Lalime himself was killed 17 June 1812; no source places a Lalime child or widow in the town on 14 August.

not_placed.name: Native children of the camps (Helm's 179 women and children)
not_placed.why: Another researcher's group by the brief.

not_placed.name: Margaret Helm (17) and Cicely
not_placed.why: Wives and women, not children: the women's researcher. Note that Darius Heald calls Cicely "a little negro slave-girl" in 1811, so she may herself have been in her teens in 1812.
